proof_skeleton_nl: Fix a prime p > 3 and define the modular inverse map I(k). Let S be the set of descent positions of the sequence I(1), I(2), ..., I(p-1). The key arithmetic input is L4: five consecutive inverse values can never be strictly increasing. By contraposition with L3, this means every four consecutive candidate positions {t,t+1,t+2,t+3} contain at least one descent, for each t from 1 to p-5. Then apply the purely combinatorial interval-hitting lemma L5 with N = p-2 and T = S to obtain |S| >= ceil((p-2)/4). Since p is odd, L6 simplifies this to |S| >= floor(p/4). Finally use floor(p/4) > p/4 - 1 to deduce |S| > p/4 - 1, which is exactly the theorem.

steps.derives: For the fixed prime p > 3, the function I : {1,...,p-1} -> {1,...,p-1} is well-defined by the rule k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p), and therefore the set S = { k in {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) } is well-defined.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the existence-and-uniqueness content of L1 together with the explicit definition of S.

steps.derives: For every integer t with 1 <= t <= p-5, at least one of t, t+1, t+2, t+3 belongs to S.
steps.trivial_justification: Assume toward contradiction that some t in {1,...,p-5} satisfies t,t+1,t+2,t+3 notin S. By L3, this would force I(t) < I(t+1) < I(t+2) < I(t+3) < I(t+4). But L4 states that no such strictly increasing five-term block can occur. Therefore every block {t,t+1,t+2,t+3} must meet S.
Apply L5 with N = p-2 and T = S. Step A2 verifies the hypothesis that every interval of four consecutive integers inside {1,...,p-2} intersects S. Hence L5 yields |S| >= ceil((p-2)/4).
Because every prime p > 3 is odd, L6 gives ceil((p-2)/4) = floor(p/4). Substitute this equality into the inequality from A3.

steps.derives: The number of integers k in {1,...,p-2} such that I(k+1) < I(k) is greater than p/4 - 1.
steps.trivial_justification: Step A4 says |S| >= floor(p/4). For every real x, floor(x) > x - 1; applying this with x = p/4 gives floor(p/4) > p/4 - 1. Therefore |S| > p/4 - 1. Since S was defined as { k in {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }, this is exactly the required theorem.
